text: fepristone also produces cervical dilatation and stimulates uterine contraction and has been tried for cervical ripening and for induction of labour. A systematic review of studies found that it may be effective, but its place in therapy has yet to be established.14 In pregnancies at term, premature rupture of the fetal membranes may be treated with early induction of labour or expectant management (waiting for labour to occur nat- urally, which will start within 24 hours in most women15). There have been concerns that prolonged rupture of mem- branes may result in higher rates of maternal and neonatal infection, but that induction may result in more caesarean deliveries.11 A systematic review15 of studies in women with premature rupture of membranes at 37 weeks or later, comparing induction (oxytocin infusion or intravaginal dinoprostone) with expectant management found no dif- ference in rates of caesarean section or instrumental vagi- nal births. There were lower rates of chorioamnionitis and endometritis in women treated with induction. In neonates, there was no difference in infection rate, but fewer admis- sions to the intensive care unit after oxytocin use. Women were also more satisfied with induction than expectant management. Oral and vaginal misoprostol have also been investigated in this group, and may have a similar efficacy to oxytocin and dinoprostone.11 Labour augmentation may be started when labour is ab- normally slow (dystocia) due to atony. Oxytocin is gener- ally used, in similar doses to those for induction.7 As for induction, both high- and low-dose regimens have been described, with higher doses reducing the duration of la- bour and rate of caesarean deliveries, but causing more hy- perstimulation.3 Augmentation using oxytocin results in normal vaginal delivery in about half of all women treat- ed.16 Intravaginal dinoprostone has also been used for augmen- tation of labour. A placebo-controlled study17 in women with slow cervical dilatation found doses of 1 or 2 mg to be effective for improving cervical dilatation and reducing the time to delivery; women given the higher dose were less likely to require oxytocin augmentation after 6 hours, but were at greater risk of hyperstimulation. Once delivery has successfully been initiated, manage- ment of the third stage of labour may be considered to re- duce the risks of postpartum haemorrhage (see below). 1. Sanchez-Ramos L.
